The word bark has several completely separate meanings as a noun. These meanings share no connection to each other — they just happen to be spelled and pronounced the same way. This is called a homonym.
1. The Outer Covering of a Tree (Primary and Most Common Meaning)

This is the meaning most people think of first, and the one you will encounter most often.

The simple definition: Bark is the tough, protective outer layer that wraps around the outside of a tree — its trunk, branches, and even roots. Think of it as the tree's "skin."

What it looks like: Bark varies enormously from tree to tree. It can be rough and deeply grooved (like on an old oak), smooth and pale (like on a beech tree), white and papery (like on a birch tree), or reddish and fibrous (like on a redwood). It is usually dry and firm to the touch.

The Two Layers of Bark

Bark is not just a single, simple layer. It is made of two distinct parts, and understanding them is key to really understanding what bark is:

Outer bark (dead bark): This is the part you see and touch. It is made entirely of dead cells, which is why you can peel or carve into it without hurting the tree directly. It acts like armor — shielding the tree from insects, fungi, disease, physical damage, and extreme weather. It also prevents the tree from losing moisture.

Inner bark (also called phloem, pronounced "flow-em"): Directly beneath the outer bark is a thin, soft, moist layer that is very much alive. Its job is to transport food — specifically, sugars produced by the leaves during photosynthesis — downward through the tree to the branches, trunk, and roots. This layer is the tree's lifeline.

Why Bark Matters So Much

Here is a fact that shows just how critical bark is: if you cut away or peel off a complete ring of bark all the way around a tree's trunk — exposing and destroying that inner layer — the tree will die. Why? Because the food made in the leaves can no longer travel down to the roots, so the roots starve. This process is called girdling, and it is one of the most effective (and destructive) ways to kill a tree. Even wildlife can accidentally girdle trees — deer rubbing their antlers on trunks, or beavers gnawing around the base.

Real-World Uses of Bark

Bark is not just important to trees — humans have found countless uses for it throughout history:

  • Spices: Cinnamon — the spice you sprinkle on your oatmeal — is literally the dried inner bark of the cinnamon tree, rolled into sticks or ground into powder.
  • Medicine: The bark of the cinchona tree produces quinine, a compound historically used to treat malaria.
  • Cork: The soft, spongy bark of the cork oak tree is harvested to make wine bottle corks, cork boards, and insulation.
  • Tanning leather: Bark from oak trees is rich in tannins, which are used to process and preserve animal hides into leather.
  • Paper and writing material: Birch bark was used for writing and making containers by indigenous peoples across the northern hemisphere.
  • Dyes and inks: Various tree barks produce natural pigments used for coloring fabrics and making inks.

Examples in Sentences

  • "The dog scraped its paw against the rough bark of the pine tree."
  • "Hikers carved their initials into the bark, which the forest ranger discouraged."
  • "Cinnamon is simply the bark of a tropical tree, dried and ground."
  • "After the wildfire, the bark on many surviving trees was charred black, but the trees were still alive."

As a noun, bark also refers to the sharp, explosive, short sound that a dog makes.

  • "The sudden bark of the neighbor's dog startled her."
  • "The puppy's bark was high-pitched and squeaky."

This same word is used for similar sounds made by other animals, such as seals and foxes, which produce a comparably sharp, abrupt sound.

Extended use — human sounds: The word can also describe a sudden, rough, sharp sound made by a person, usually in speech or laughter:

  • "He let out a bark of laughter" — meaning a sudden, loud, abrupt laugh.
  • "Her bark silenced the entire room" — meaning a sharp, commanding shout.

This usage usually implies that the sound was abrupt and a little harsh, like a command.
3. A Type of Sailing Ship (also spelled "barque")

In older, nautical (sea-related) language, a bark or barque is a specific type of sailing vessel with three or more masts. Its defining feature is how its sails are arranged: the front masts are rigged with square sails (set across the ship), while the rearmost mast carries fore-and-aft sails (set along the length of the ship).

This is not a meaning you will encounter in everyday modern conversation. You are most likely to come across it when reading classic literature, historical novels, or texts about maritime history.

  • "The bark set sail before sunrise, heading south toward the cape."

In the world of food and sweets, bark refers to a type of confection made by spreading melted chocolate in a thin, flat layer on a surface, adding toppings such as nuts, dried fruit, crushed candy canes, or sea salt, and then allowing it to harden and cool.

The resulting slab is then broken by hand into irregular, jagged pieces — and those uneven, rough-edged pieces look remarkably like broken chunks of tree bark. That is exactly where the name comes from.

  • "She prepared a tray of dark chocolate bark with pistachios and dried cranberries."
  • "Peppermint bark is a popular holiday treat."

So the noun bark carries four distinct meanings:

First and most importantly, it is the protective outer covering of a tree — a layered structure with a tough, dead outer shell and a living, food-carrying inner layer. It is the tree's skin, armor, and transport system all in one.

Second, it is the sharp, sudden sound a dog (or similar animal, or even a person) makes.

Third, it is an old term for a specific type of multi-masted sailing ship.

Fourth, in cooking, it is a flat, hardened slab of chocolate broken into rough pieces.

In most everyday situations — reading, writing, or conversation — when you see or hear the word bark used as a noun, context will tell you almost instantly which meaning is intended. A sentence about trees? Tree bark. A sentence about dogs? The sound. A sentence about dessert? The chocolate treat. And the ship meaning is rare enough that you will almost always see it in a clearly historical or literary context.
